title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
hook: Brahma and Vishnu are arguing about which of them is greater when a pillar of fire splits the sky between them

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum, and the goddess's part of the year, with tools resting under flowers. Which tool did you clean? Today the year turns to Shiva. Day one thousand one hundred eighteen.

Two gods are arguing. Brahma, the creator, says he's the greatest, since everything came from him. Vishnu, the preserver, says no, he is, since he keeps everything going. The argument gets hot. The other gods get nervous. And then, between the two of them, a pillar of fire appears. It's blazing. It goes up past where they can see and down past where they can see. It has no top in sight and no bottom. Both gods stop mid-sentence and stare at it. That's one of the stories the Shiva Purana tells, and it's where this new part of the year begins.
screen: `TWO GODS ARGUING.` → `A PILLAR OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: The Shiva Purana is a big book of stories about Shiva, his worship and the people around him. It presents itself as told aloud: a storyteller named Suta recounting it to a gathering of sages. Over the next days we'll take selections, not the whole. Back to the pillar. The two gods agree on a test. Whoever finds the end of this thing wins. Vishnu takes the form of a boar and starts digging down. Brahma takes the form of a swan and flies up. They go a very long way. Vishnu digs and digs and finds no bottom, and finally he comes back and says so. He couldn't find the end. Brahma flies and flies and finds no top. But on the way he meets a ketaki flower drifting down, and he has an idea. He comes back and says he reached the top, and he brings the flower along to swear it's true. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out of it. Shiva honors Vishnu for telling the truth. He rebukes Brahma for the lie, and in the story the ketaki flower, the false witness, is not to be offered in Shiva's worship. Here's what makes the story worth carrying. The point isn't who won. Nobody found the end. For Shaiva devotees, the linga in a Shiva temple recalls this pillar: something that can't be measured from either side. And the one who comes out of the story well is the one who came back and admitted it. I looked, I couldn't find the end. Before something that big, the story honors the honest answer and rebukes the one who pretended to have it figured out.
screen: `A BOOK OF SHIVA'S STORIES.` · `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` · `ONE ADMITS IT, ONE LIES.` · `A PILLAR NO ONE CAN MEASURE.` · then, large: `I COULDN'T FIND THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: rest in not knowing. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one big question you don't have an answer to. Where something comes from. What happens to someone you love. Why things are the way they are. Don't try to reach the top or the bottom of it. Let it stand in front of you like the pillar, too big to measure. Breathe in. Breathe out. If a quick answer comes, let it go by, like the flower drifting down. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, and leave the question with it. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Purana. A book of Shiva's stories, told by Suta to the sages, and one of them is a pillar of fire that no one could measure.
Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. Today, when you don't know something, say so plainly, once, the way Vishnu did. Day one thousand one hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Shaiva Hindus worship Shiva in the form of the linga in temples and homes, and the story of the endless pillar of fire is told and carved in temples as the appearance of the linga, Lingodbhava; it is also linked to Maha Shivaratri.

notes: First day of the Shiva part (1118–1124 are the Shiva Purana selections). This writer's selections: 1118 the pillar of fire (Vidyeshvara Samhita); 1119 Sati and Daksha's sacrifice; 1120 Kama burned; 1121 Parvati's tapas and the disguised visitor (all Rudra Samhita). 1122–1124 belong to another writer.

Pillar story details: the quarrel over greatness, the fiery column, Vishnu as boar digging down, Brahma as swan flying up, the ketaki flower as false witness, Shiva emerging, Vishnu honored, Brahma rebuked, ketaki excluded from Shiva's worship. Paraphrased; confirm against the Vidyeshvara Samhita. The Bhairava episode (Brahma's fifth head) is omitted.
'Like other Puranas, it presents itself as told aloud by Suta to sages': confirm the frame for the Shiva Purana.
Linga 'recalls' the pillar is offered as the story's own link; Shaiva theologies of the linga vary. Confirm phrasing; the link to Maha Shivaratri appears only in howItsDone.
Original note glosses Purana as 'a book of old stories'; confirm.

Editor pass: cut 'like other Puranas' (an unsourced generalization); the linga link now attributed to Shaiva devotees rather than stated by the narrator; the closing moral ('honesty is the right answer') recast as what the story honors and rebukes, so the narrator isn't preaching; practice phrased as an invitation.
